<p class="lead-statement">A map is an argument. I teach students to make one they can defend.</p>

I teach environmental questions by connecting physical processes with the decisions people make about them. My university teaching so far has been as a Graduate Teaching Assistant at the University of Guelph (September 2022–April 2024), where I led laboratories and supported assessment in undergraduate physical geography and GIS courses. I have not yet been an instructor of record.

## Teaching philosophy {#teaching-philosophy}

Students learn environmental science best when they work on a real question with real data and have to defend what they conclude. Three commitments follow from that.

<div class="cards three compact-cards"><article class="research-card"><h3>Start from a problem</h3><p>A GIS operation or a hydrological concept makes sense once it answers a question. In labs I introduce the question first (where is erosion risk highest, and why?) and then the tool that addresses it.</p></article><article class="research-card"><h3>Reason, then click</h3><p>Software changes; spatial thinking lasts. I ask students to say what they expect a result to look like before they run an analysis, and to explain any difference afterwards. Troubleshooting becomes part of the learning.</p></article><article class="research-card"><h3>Feedback students can use</h3><p>Comments on lab work should show how to improve the next submission, not only justify a grade. I write feedback that names what worked, what did not, and what to try next.</p></article></div>

I also try to make it easy to ask for help. Lab groups include students with very different levels of technical confidence, and many will not raise a hand. I move around the room and go to students, and I keep instructions available in writing as well as spoken.

My professional background shapes what I bring into the classroom. Before my PhD I spent six years in climate adaptation and development work in Bangladesh, at BRAC and the International Centre for Climate Change and Development (ICCCAD). Those cases let me show students how environmental evidence is used, contested and sometimes ignored when decisions are made, alongside examples from Ontario watersheds.

Students know me as Zion, the name used in these comments.

### What I changed

Feedback from my first winter of lab teaching (GEOG\*1300, Winter 2023) was more mixed. Some students said I moved through lab material too quickly and did not make the requirements clear enough. I now plan pacing first: short written instructions, a worked example before students start, and deliberate pauses for questions. Comments from the following year describe the background explanations as easy to understand. The groups were different and the samples small, so I treat this as encouragement, not proof.

The first group rests on courses I have supported as a teaching assistant. The second rests on my research and professional record; I have not yet taught these as courses. At graduate level I could contribute to seminars on environmental modelling, spatial decision support and research design.

## Mentoring {#mentoring}

I have not yet formally supervised graduate students. My mentoring experience so far comes from four settings: mentoring a summer research student in our research group at Guelph; one-to-one support for undergraduates in labs and office hours; guiding junior colleagues' research papers, policy briefs and reports while coordinating the research portfolio at ICCCAD; and staff and stakeholder training at BRAC and ICCCAD. In 2023 I represented graduate students on a University of Guelph faculty search committee, which showed me how departments weigh teaching and mentoring.

<div class="evidence-panel mentoring-case"><p class="eyebrow">Research mentoring · Summer 2025 · University of Guelph</p><h3>From summer student to co-author</h3><p>From May 2025 I mentored Mckenna Thompson, a summer research student in our group. She worked with me on my field-level precision-conservation study and is a co-author of the resulting paper in <em>International Soil and Water Conservation Research</em> (2026, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.iswcr.2026.100668">doi:10.1016/j.iswcr.2026.100668</a>). She is now an M.Sc. student in Earth Sciences at the University of Waterloo.</p></div>

<figure class="feedback-card"><blockquote>“I had the opportunity of seeing his work on a project from the very early planning stages through to its completion. … It’s been a pleasure learning from you, Zion!”</blockquote><figcaption>Mckenna Thompson, summer research student, 2025 · LinkedIn recommendation, September 2025</figcaption></figure>

As a supervisor I would build on that experience: give students a defined question within the [research program](research.qmd#five-year-program), early experience with real partner data, regular written feedback, and authorship when their contribution earns it. I would expect to learn the formal role with guidance from experienced colleagues.
